title: Providence
hook: Calvin: nothing happens by chance; God holds all things

segments.voice: Yesterday, the theology of the cross. Your line was God hidden in weakness. Where did you look for God inside something hard? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

Joseph's brothers stand in front of him in Egypt, terrified. Long ago they threw him into a pit and sold him. Now he's the man who decides whether their families eat. Their father has just died, and they're sure revenge is coming. Joseph weeps. Then he tells them: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." One event, two intentions inside it. John Calvin built a whole teaching on lines like that, under the name providence.

Calvin taught that nothing happens by chance. The world isn't a machine God wound up and walked away from, and it isn't a dice game either. God holds all things and steers them. He leaned on Jesus's words about sparrows sold in the market: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered." And on a proverb: "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD." Even a cast lot, the proverb says, doesn't fall outside God's hand. For Calvin this wasn't a cold idea to argue about. He wrote that knowing God's providence brings thankfulness when things go well, patience when they don't, and freedom from anxiety about what's coming. If the future is in God's hand, he reasoned, a believer doesn't have to hold all of it alone. Christians understand providence in different ways. Reformed churches follow Calvin closely, with strong words about God's governing of every event. Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist and other Christians also confess God's providence, while describing human freedom and chance in their own ways. And they read the same Joseph. Notice when he says his line. Not from the bottom of the pit, but years later, looking back over the whole road. Providence in Genesis is something Joseph sees in the rearview mirror. While it was happening, it only looked like a pit.

Here's the practice: trust one uncertain thing to God. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you can't control. A test result. A decision someone else will make. A child far away. Money that may or may not come. Notice how your hands want to grip it. Let them open on your lap. If you pray, you can hand that one thing to God, the way Calvin pictured it: held in a hand bigger than yours. If you don't pray, simply notice what it's like to set it down for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Providence. Calvin's teaching that God holds and steers all things, so that nothing happens by chance.
Your line: held in his hand. Today, when that uncertain thing comes back to mind, open your hand for one breath. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians speak of God's providence in prayer and in hard times, often with Joseph's words from Genesis 50:20; Reformed churches teach it in Calvin's strong form, and other churches confess it while describing human freedom in their own ways.

notes: Calvin is paraphrased; the fruits of providence (gratitude, patience, freedom from worry about the future) follow Institutes I.17.7–11. Confirm.
Calvin's use of Matthew 10:29 and Proverbs 16:33 in Institutes I.16 should be confirmed.
The sentence on Catholic, Orthodox and Methodist views is deliberately general; confirm it is fair to each.
'Long ago' and 'years later' are left unquantified on purpose (Genesis gives the timeline only indirectly).

Editor pass: cut the superlatives 'one of the strangest sentences in Genesis' and 'the cheapest birds'; 'roll of the dice' now 'cast lot' to match Proverbs 16:33; the line about the future now speaks in Calvin's voice, not the narrator's; varied the hook's closing line.
Audit (fresh reviewer): Genesis 50:20, Matthew 10:29–30 and Proverbs 16:33 checked against the KJV; Calvin's use of them in Institutes I.16 confirmed; no change needed.
